job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today we are discussing the Mahajanapadas. Rohan, why did Magadha become so powerful? Rohan: I think it was because they had the best swords and magic weapons. Teacher: Not quite. Magadha was powerful because the rivers Ganga and Son provided water, transport, and helped in land defense. Also, iron ore mines were nearby, which were used to make strong tools for clearing forests and farming, not just weapons. Priya: What about the taxes? Did farmers pay with paper money? Teacher: No, they paid a share of their produce, usually one-sixth of what they grew, known as bhaga. Sometimes, laborers had to work for the king for one day every month as a form of labor tax. Rohan: And what about the Vajji republic? Was it a perfect democracy where everyone voted? Teacher: Actually, it was a Gana or Sangha, where many rulers met in assemblies to discuss matters, but not every single person had a vote. Finally, remember that the Ashvamedha was a ritual sacrifice where a horse was let loose to wander, and the king had to protect it to show his authority, not a simple race to find the fastest horse.

items.evidence: Magadha was powerful because the rivers Ganga and Son provided water, transport, and helped in land defense.
items.q: Why did the rivers Ganga and Son help Magadha become strong?
options: They gave transport and helped defend the land
They gave drinking water to its soldiers only
They made its kings very brave in battle
They gave it iron ore for making swords
items.explain: The rivers gave water and transport, and helped defend the land, so Magadha grew powerful.

wrong.why: thinks the rivers were only for drinking water
thinks Magadha won only through brave kings
thinks iron was only for weapons and mixes up the source

items.evidence: Also, iron ore mines were nearby, which were used to make strong tools for clearing forests and farming, not just weapons.
items.q: Which use of iron in Magadha shows it was not only for war?
options: Making tools to clear forests and farm
Making shields for the king's guards
Making swords for the army's soldiers
Making walls to defend the capital city
items.explain: Iron was also used for strong tools to clear forests and farm, not just for weapons.

wrong.why: thinks iron was used only for war gear
thinks iron meant swords for soldiers
links iron to forts and showing power

items.evidence: Sometimes, laborers had to work for the king for one day every month as a form of labor tax.
items.q: A laborer works one day each month for the king. How is this seen?
options: As a tax paid with labour
As a punishment for breaking rules
As a fee paid in paper money
As a gift given to the Ashvamedha
items.explain: Working one day a month for the king was a labor tax, not a punishment.

wrong.why: thinks the work was a punishment
thinks taxes were paid in paper money
mixes the labour tax up with the Ashvamedha ritual

items.evidence: Actually, it was a Gana or Sangha, where many rulers met in assemblies to discuss matters, but not every single person had a vote.
items.q: How was the Vajji republic different from a rule where everyone votes?
options: Many rulers met to discuss, not all voted
One king decided and nobody could speak
Every farmer voted, but rulers did not meet
All people voted in one huge assembly
items.explain: Vajji was a Gana or Sangha where many rulers met in assemblies, but not everyone had a vote.

wrong.why: thinks a republic meant rule by one king
reverses who met and who voted
